```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(error = TRUE)
```

Work through this file alongside the chapter "Null Distributions" in the book. Keep it in the same folder as your `my_functions.R`.

## Load your toolbox

```{r load-toolbox}
library(tidyverse)
source("my_functions.R")

scores <- c(44, 47, 48, 49, 50, 50, 51, 52, 53, 56)

all.equal(my_mean(scores), mean(scores))
all.equal(my_t_value(scores, 49), unname(t.test(scores, mu = 49)$statistic))
```

You are looking for two `TRUE`s. If you see `could not find function`, finish the toolbox section at the end of the "The One-Sample t-Test" exercise file first.

## A world where the null is true

Steves are exactly average here: their heights have a mean of 175 cm and an SD of 7 cm, the same as everyone else's. Run this chunk a few times. The heights change, and so does the t-value against 175.

```{r one-null-sample}
null_sample <- rnorm(n = 10, mean = 175, sd = 7)
null_sample

my_t_value(null_sample, comparison_value = 175)
```

## Many groups of Steves

1000 groups of 10 Steves, keeping each group's mean height. Compare the SD of the means with the standard error.

```{r null-means}
null_means <- replicate(1000, mean(rnorm(n = 10, mean = 175, sd = 7)))

c(sd_of_means = my_sd(null_means), formula_se = 7 / sqrt(10))

hist(null_means, breaks = 40)
```

```{r my-null-t}
my_null_t(n = 10, pop_mean = 175, pop_sd = 7)
```

### Check it against R

```{r my-null-t-check}
set.seed(1)
mine <- my_null_t(n = 10, pop_mean = 175, pop_sd = 7)

set.seed(1)
r_version <- unname(
  t.test(rnorm(n = 10, mean = 175, sd = 7), mu = 175)$statistic
)

c(mine = mine, R = r_version)
all.equal(mine, r_version)
```

## Many t-values

```{r null-ts}
null_ts <- replicate(1000, my_null_t(n = 10, pop_mean = 175, pop_sd = 7))

hist(null_ts, breaks = 40)
```

## Where do the rare values start?

```{r sorted-ts}
sorted_ts <- sort(null_ts)

head(sorted_ts)
tail(sorted_ts)
```

### Your turn: pick them out by position

To mark the rarest 5% of 1000 t-values, 25 go in each tail. The lower cutoff is the 26th smallest value and the upper cutoff is the 975th.

```{r cutoffs-by-position}
lower <-
upper <-

c(lower = lower, upper = upper)
```

### See the rare values

Set `alpha_choice` to 0.5, 0.1, 0.05 and 0.01, and run the chunk each time.

```{r rare-plot}
alpha_choice <- 0.05
rare_cutoffs <- my_cutoffs(null_ts, alpha = alpha_choice)

null_t_data <- tibble(t = null_ts) %>%
  mutate(rare = t < rare_cutoffs[1] | t > rare_cutoffs[2])

ggplot(null_t_data, aes(x = t, fill = rare)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = rare_cutoffs, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "#467AAC", "TRUE" = "#D55E00"),
                    guide = "none") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-6, 6)) +
  labs(x = "t-value", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()

null_t_data %>%
  summarise(beyond = sum(rare), share = mean(rare))
```

### Compare with R

```{r cutoffs-compare}
tibble(
  cutoff = c("lower", "upper"),
  simulated = my_cutoffs(null_ts),
  qt = qt(c(0.025, 0.975), df = 9)
)
```

## Rare, but not impossible

How many of your 1000 groups of Steves averaged more than 180 cm, or less than 170 cm?

```{r rare-groups}
sum(null_means > 180)
sum(null_means < 170)
```

## Add to your toolbox

1. Open `my_functions.R`.
2. Copy your finished `my_null_t()` and `my_cutoffs()` into it, under the **Null Distributions** heading. Copy only the functions.
3. Save `my_functions.R`.

Now check that the saved toolbox works on its own. You are looking for two `TRUE`s.

```{r toolbox-check}
rm(list = ls())
source("my_functions.R")

set.seed(1)
mine <- my_null_t(n = 10, pop_mean = 175, pop_sd = 7)
set.seed(1)
r_version <- unname(
  t.test(rnorm(n = 10, mean = 175, sd = 7), mu = 175)$statistic
)
all.equal(mine, r_version)

# 20:1 counts down from 20 to 1; with alpha = 0.1, one value is in each tail
all.equal(my_cutoffs(20:1, alpha = 0.1), c(2, 19))
```

If you see `could not find function`, that function is not in `my_functions.R` yet, or the file was not saved.
